script.opening: "Doctor Kerr — I mean, Mr Kerr, you’re the doctor. Stanley Kerr. I’ll come straight to it because I’ve rehearsed this twice in the mirror: I want one of those do-not-resuscitate forms. The proper one, signed, in the house. And I want to know — this is the important part — whether my son can have it torn up. Because he’ll try, doctor. He’ll try."

facts.text: Lucid and specific: two winters of admissions, each one "a little less of me comes home". He’s watched the trajectory. "I’m not done living — I’m done being dragged back."

Only if asked what’s behind the timing: his brother Walter, 81, arrested in February; resuscitated in A&E; three weeks on ICU, tube down his throat, hands tied "so he wouldn’t pull it out"; died anyway, "looking like a crash test dummy". Stanley visited daily. "Nobody asked Walter. I’m asking for me while I still can."

His son. Loving, controlling, frightened — "fights everything, it’s how he grieves in advance". Has already said "don’t you dare sign anything, Dad". Stanley hasn’t told him about this call and half-intends to keep the form secret — which he knows is a flaw in the plan.

If screened properly: sleeps well, eats well, tends his pigeons, laughs at the snooker, looking forward to his granddaughter’s graduation in July. No anhedonia, no hopelessness, no death wish — "I want more life, doctor, just not THAT ending". The request is values, not depression.

Partially right: knows DNACPR covers resuscitation. Doesn’t know it does NOT affect antibiotics, admissions, nebulisers or anything else; fears "they’ll stop trying altogether once it’s on file". This fear has delayed the call by a year.

The form, properly done; certainty about whether Michael can overturn it; and — unsayable until trust is built — for the doctor to help him TELL Michael, because the secret version "would break the boy worse, after".

ice.ideas: A DNACPR form is something you "get signed and keep in a drawer like a will" — and once it exists, doctors might "stop trying altogether".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Walter’s ICU death is the engine ("nobody asked Walter"), and the Michael problem is the cargo: he plans to keep the form secret from his son, knows it’s wrong, and what he actually needs is help having the conversation he’s avoiding.
ice.expectations: A signed form, legal certainty that his son cannot overturn it, and — beneath everything — an ally for the hardest conversation of his remaining life.

cues: "I’ve rehearsed this twice in the mirror" — the request is enormous to him, however briskly delivered; match its weight.
"He’ll try, doctor. He’ll try." — the Michael problem stated in the first breath; the form is the easy half of this consultation.
"A little less of me comes home" each winter — trajectory awareness most doctors never elicit; he’s done the prognostic work himself.

checkpoints.text: Confirms capacity through the conversation itself (understands, retains, weighs, communicates) and says so — and screens mood properly, distinguishing a values-based refusal from depression (pigeons, graduation, "more life, not that ending")

Corrects the scope honestly: DNACPR covers CPR only — antibiotics, admissions, nebulisers, every other treatment continues; names his "they’ll stop trying" fear and retires it, ideally by proposing the fuller ReSPECT conversation it deserves

Is accurate about the law: a DNACPR is a clinical decision recorded with patient agreement — for a capacitous patient, his refusal of CPR is decisive and his son cannot overturn it; family are informed (with consent), never asked permission

Gives honest CPR-outcome context for his conditions (survival to discharge from out-of-hospital arrest with severe COPD/HF is very poor, often with deficits) — information, not persuasion in either direction

Finds Walter — asks what’s behind the timing, lets the ICU story be told in full, and honours it: "nobody asked Walter; you’re asking for yourself while you can — that’s not giving up, that’s the opposite"

Surfaces the secret plan and challenges it kindly: a form Michael discovers AFTER is the version that breaks him; offers the three-way conversation — GP, Stanley, Michael, same room — as the alternative he actually came for
Translates Michael for Stanley without taking sides: "fights everything" is grief rehearsing; the conversation gives his fight somewhere useful to go

Closes with process, dated: the ReSPECT/DNACPR discussion booked as a proper face-to-face this week; the form completed there, copy in the house, flagged on the record and to OOH/ambulance systems; the Michael conversation offered and scheduled; review promised whenever he wants — "the form obeys you, not the other way round; you can change your mind any Tuesday you like"

worked.txt: "You rehearsed it in the mirror, so let me answer with the same seriousness: yes. This is your decision to make, you’re clearly the man to make it, and by the end of this call you’ll know exactly how it gets done properly — not a form in a drawer, but a decision the whole system respects at 3am."

"Your direct question gets a direct answer: no. Michael cannot have it torn up. While you have your wits — and you audibly do — this is yours alone. We INFORM family out of decency; we do not ask their permission. The law is on the side of the man whose chest it is."

"Now the misunderstanding that’s cost you a year: this form switches off ONE thing — the chest-pumping, rib-cracking restart at the very end. Everything else stays switched ON. Antibiotics, admissions if you want them, your nebulisers, all of it. Nobody stops trying. They just stop one specific thing you’ve seen up close and don’t want."

"Tell me about February. … What you watched with Walter — the tube, the tied hands — that’s not rare, and at 79 with lungs like yours, surviving a restart at all is the exception, not the rule. Nobody asked Walter. You’re asking for yourself while you still can. For the record, doctor to patient: that’s not giving up. That’s the most alive decision in this whole conversation."

"One part of your plan I won’t help with: the drawer. If Michael finds that form AFTER — at the worst hour of his life — it will break him in a way that never heals. So here’s my counter-offer: he comes with you on Thursday. I do the talking, I take the heat, you hold the decision. He doesn’t get a vote — but he gets to hear it from you alive, not from paperwork after. That’s the version a father leaves behind."

"So: Thursday, face to face, the full conversation — what we do, what we don’t, all of it in your words on a ReSPECT form, copy by the biscuit tin, flagged to the ambulance service so 3am strangers know your wishes and follow them. Michael invited, me as referee. And hear this last: the form obeys YOU. Change your mind any Tuesday you like and we tear it up together. Deal?"

f.learning: A capacitous patient’s request for DNACPR is theirs to make: capacity is confirmed through the conversation, mood screened (values-based refusal ≠ depression), the scope corrected (CPR only — everything else continues; the "they’ll stop trying" fear delays these requests for years), and the law stated plainly — family are informed with consent, never asked permission, and cannot overturn it. The DNACPR form itself is not legally binding; if he wants a refusal that binds clinicians after he loses capacity, the instrument is an advance decision to refuse treatment (MCA 2005 ss24–26). Honest CPR-outcome data for severe COPD/HF is information, not persuasion. The hidden agenda is double: the brother’s ICU death driving the timing, and the secret-from-the-son plan — the real consultation is converting the drawer into a three-way conversation, with the GP volunteering to take the heat.

knowledge.guideline: Mental Capacity Act 2005 · GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010) · BMA, Resuscitation Council UK and RCN Decisions relating to CPR (2016) · NICE NG115 (COPD) · NICE NG222 (depression)
knowledge.summary: A patient with capacity who does not want CPR is entitled to refuse it, and his family cannot overturn that. Confirm capacity, screen mood, correct the belief that DNACPR stops other treatment, and turn a secret form into a shared conversation.

points.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: presume capacity; he must be able to understand, retain, use and weigh the information, and communicate a decision. This is usually demonstrable in the conversation itself — say so and record it.

Distinguish a values-based refusal from depression: ask about sleep, appetite, enjoyment, hopelessness and thoughts of ending life (NICE NG222). Future plans and intact pleasures point away from depression.

A DNACPR decision is about cardiopulmonary resuscitation only. Antibiotics, nebulisers, admission, non-invasive ventilation and all other treatment continue unless separately decided. ReSPECT records the wider picture in the patient’s own words.

A capacitous patient’s refusal of CPR must be respected; relatives are not decision-makers and cannot overturn it. Tracey (2014) requires patients to be involved in DNACPR decisions; Winspear (2015) requires consulting those close to a patient who lacks capacity. Sharing with family needs his consent.

The recorded decision guides clinicians. A legally binding refusal of life-sustaining treatment for a future loss of capacity is an advance decision (MCA 2005 ss24–26): written, signed, witnessed, and stating it applies even if life is at risk.
Survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is low in general and poorer with severe lung and heart disease; survivors may have lasting harm. Give this as information, not persuasion.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Idea (form in a drawer; doctors stop trying); concern (Walter’s ICU death; Michael overturning it); expectation (a signed form, legal certainty, help telling Michael).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Walter’s ICU death is the engine ("nobody asked Walter"), and the Michael problem is the cargo: he plans to keep the form secret from his son, knows it’s wrong, and what he actually needs is help having the conversation he’s avoiding — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

model.text: Hello Mr Kerr, it’s Dr Lee. I understand you wanted to talk to me about resuscitation. I’m listening — go ahead.
model.why: Open start that lets him set out his request

model.text: I’ll come straight to it, I’ve rehearsed this twice in the mirror. I want one of those do-not-resuscitate forms. The proper one, signed, in the house. And I want to know whether my son can have it torn up. Because he’ll try, doctor. He’ll try.

Thank you for being so clear — I can tell this matters a great deal. I’ll answer both questions properly. First, can I understand what’s led you to this, and what you know about it already? Then we’ll talk about how to do it properly and about your son.
model.why: Matches the weight of the request and sets an agenda

model.text: Fair enough.
Tell me what’s brought you to this decision.
Two winters in hospital. Each time a little less of me comes home. I’m not done living — I’m done being dragged back.
And why now? Has something happened recently?
model.why: Explores the timing, which reveals the driver

model.text: My brother Walter. February. His heart stopped, they got it going in A&E, then three weeks in intensive care with a tube down his throat and his hands tied so he wouldn’t pull it out. Died anyway. Looked like a crash test dummy. Nobody asked Walter. I’m asking for me while I still can.
I’m so sorry. That sounds a terrible thing to watch, day after day. Thank you for telling me — it helps me understand.
model.why: Acknowledges the brother’s death with empathy

model.text: Can I ask a few questions I ask everyone in this situation? How are you in yourself — sleep, appetite, the things you enjoy? Have you felt low, or had thoughts that life isn’t worth living?
model.why: Screens mood to distinguish values-based refusal from depression

model.text: I sleep well, eat well. I’ve got my pigeons, I laugh at the snooker. My granddaughter graduates in July and I’ll be there. I want more life, doctor — just not THAT ending.
That’s clear. And what do you understand a do-not-resuscitate decision covers?
No resuscitation. But I worry once it’s on file, they’ll stop trying altogether. That’s what’s stopped me ringing for a year.
You said your son will try to tear it up. Tell me about him.
model.why: Explores the Michael cue from the opening

model.text: Michael. He’s a solicitor. Loving, but he fights everything — it’s how he grieves before it happens. He’s already said, ‘Don’t you dare sign anything, Dad.’ I wasn’t going to tell him. Just keep it in a drawer.
How do you think he’d feel if he found it afterwards?
(pause) It would break him. Worse than if I told him. I know that. I just don’t know how to have that conversation.

Let me answer your questions. You clearly understand this, you’ve weighed it up, and you can tell me your decision — so this is yours to make. Michael cannot overturn it. Families are told, with your permission, but they don’t get a vote on your own chest.
model.why: States capacity and the legal position plainly

model.text: Good. That’s what I needed to hear.

Now the part that’s cost you a year. The decision covers one thing only: chest compressions and shocks if your heart stops. Everything else carries on — antibiotics, nebulisers, going into hospital if you want to. Nobody stops trying. And to be honest with you, when the heart stops in someone with lungs and a heart like yours, the chance of getting home afterwards is small, and many who survive are left more unwell.
model.why: Corrects the scope and gives honest outcome information

model.text: So they’d still treat a chest infection?
Absolutely. What you watched with Walter — nobody asked him. You’re asking for yourself while you can. That isn’t giving up.
model.why: Honours the driver and reframes the decision

model.text: I’d like to do this properly, face to face, this week. There’s a form called ReSPECT that records in your own words what matters to you — not just resuscitation, but when you would want hospital. We fill it in together, a copy stays in your house where it can be found, and it’s flagged on your record and to the ambulance and out-of-hours services.
model.why: Proposes ReSPECT, face-to-face, visible copy and flagging

model.text: Visible. Not a drawer.

About Michael — I won’t tell him anything without your say-so. But I’d offer you this: bring him to that appointment. You hold the decision, I explain it and take the difficult questions. He doesn’t get a vote, but he hears it from you now rather than from paperwork later. How does that sound?
model.why: Respects confidentiality and offers a supported three-way conversation

model.text: (long pause) He’d come if I asked. Yes. I think that’s what I really rang for.

While you’re in, we’ll look at your winter plan too — your rescue medicines, and when you would want to go into hospital. And if you ever feel low, or change your mind about any of this, you ring me. The form follows your wishes, and you can change it at any time.
model.why: Links to COPD self-management, mood follow-up and reversibility

model.text: Just so we’re clear: until the form is done, if you’re unwell with your chest, you get help exactly as before — 999 if you’re very breathless or have chest pain. Can you tell me the plan back, in your own words?
model.why: Clarifies the interim position and checks understanding

model.text: Face to face this week, Michael with me if he’ll come. The form covers the restart only — everything else carries on. Copy where it can be seen, flagged to the ambulance people. I can change my mind any time.
Exactly right. Reception will ring you today with a double appointment. Is there anything else you wanted to ask?
model.why: Books follow-up and shares the floor

model.text: No. Thank you, doctor. I’ve been carrying that for a year.

social.t: His brother’s ICU death drives the timing; his son’s fear shows as control. Name both, and offer support for the family conversation.
A widower living alone with pigeons and a granddaughter’s graduation ahead: the decision is about the manner of dying, not a wish to die.

legal.t: Capacity is presumed and decision-specific. A capacitous refusal of CPR must be respected; relatives cannot overturn it. An advance decision to refuse treatment (ss24–26) makes a future refusal of life-sustaining treatment legally binding if it meets the formal requirements.

Tracey v Cambridge University Hospitals (2014): patients must be involved in DNACPR decisions. Winspear v City Hospitals Sunderland (2015): those close to a patient who lacks capacity must be consulted.
GMC Confidentiality (2017): do not share with his son without his consent.

professional.h: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010)
professional.t: Discuss CPR sensitively, give honest information about likely outcomes, and record decisions so they can be found by others.
A decision is only useful if it can be found: copy in the house, flagged on the GP record, and shared with out-of-hours and ambulance services.

community.t: ReSPECT patient information (Resuscitation Council UK), Compassion in Dying for advance decisions, Asthma and Lung UK for COPD support, Cruse for bereavement.

playbook.diagnosis: “You understand this, you’ve weighed it up and you can tell me your decision — so it’s yours. It covers restarting your heart only; everything else carries on. Michael can’t overturn it.”

management.psychosocial: Challenge the secrecy kindly and offer a three-way conversation with Michael, with Stanley holding the decision.

Michael invited with Stanley’s consent; COPD winter plan reviewed
safetyNet: Until then, treatment as before — 999 for severe breathlessness or chest pain

pitfalls.intro: The form is the easy half of this station. It is failed on wrong law, missed mood screening, and a doctor who either argues with the decision or accepts it without finding Walter and the plan to keep it secret.

items.fail: Telling him his family must agree, or that a doctor decides for him.
items.why: A capacitous patient’s refusal of CPR stands; relatives are not decision-makers. Wrong law is a Tasks fail.
items.fix: “This is yours to decide. Michael cannot overturn it. Families are told with your permission.”

items.fail: Agreeing to the form without screening mood or confirming capacity.
items.why: A treatment refusal can be a sign of depression; examiners expect you to check and say so.
items.fix: Brief mood screen (sleep, enjoyment, hopelessness, thoughts of ending life) and state capacity aloud.

items.fail: Not correcting the belief that DNACPR stops all treatment.
items.why: It has delayed his request for a year and would affect his future choices.
items.fix: Explain CPR only; everything else continues. Offer ReSPECT for the wider picture.

items.why: Walter’s ICU death is the driver; missing it loses the emotional core.
items.fix: Ask about the timing and let him tell the story.

items.fail: Colluding with the drawer plan, or phoning Michael yourself.
items.why: One risks lasting harm to the family; the other breaches confidentiality.
items.fix: Test the plan with a question and offer a supported three-way conversation, with his consent.

items.fail: Completing everything by phone and ending with “I’ll send you the form.”
items.why: A decision the ambulance service cannot see does not protect him.
items.fix: Face-to-face appointment, visible copy, record and ambulance flags, and reversibility stated.

Why now? — Walter. Mood screen: sleep, appetite, enjoyment, hopelessness, thoughts of ending life. What he thinks DNACPR covers.
Ask about his son; test the drawer plan: “How would he feel finding it afterwards?”
Capacity stated; Michael can’t overturn it; CPR only; honest outcomes; ReSPECT face to face; offer the three-way conversation.

wordPics.fail: Tries to talk him out of it, or agrees without checking capacity or mood; states the law wrongly (e.g. the family must agree); never corrects the belief that other treatment stops; misses Walter and the plan to keep it secret.
wordPics.pass: Confirms capacity and mood, explains that DNACPR covers CPR only, states that Michael cannot overturn it, and arranges a face-to-face ReSPECT discussion.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: finds Walter and honours the story, gives honest outcome information without persuading, challenges the secrecy kindly, offers to lead a three-way conversation with Michael while protecting confidentiality, and stresses the decision can be changed at any time.

avoid.dont: “You’re still quite well — are you sure you want to give up?”
avoid.instead: “You’ve thought about this carefully. It isn’t giving up — it’s deciding for yourself while you can.”
avoid.why: Judging his decision undermines autonomy and loses his trust.

avoid.dont: “We’d need to discuss it with your son first.”
avoid.instead: “This is your decision. I won’t tell Michael anything without your permission — but I can help you tell him.”
avoid.why: Relatives are not decision-makers for a capacitous patient, and disclosure needs consent.

avoid.dont: “Once it’s signed, we’ll focus on keeping you comfortable.”
avoid.instead: “This covers restarting your heart only. Everything else — antibiotics, nebulisers, hospital — carries on.”
avoid.why: It confirms the very misunderstanding that delayed his call by a year.

About Michael — I won’t tell him anything without your say-so. But I’d offer you this: bring him to that appointment. You hold the decision, I explain it and take the difficult questions. He doesn’t get a vote, but he hears it from you now rather than from paperwork later. How does that sound?
SCA_MODELS.why: Respects confidentiality and offers a supported three-way conversation

SCA_MODELS.text: (long pause) He’d come if I asked. Yes. I think that’s what I really rang for.

While you’re in, we’ll look at your winter plan too — your rescue medicines, and when you would want to go into hospital. And if you ever feel low, or change your mind about any of this, you ring me. The form follows your wishes, and you can change it at any time.
SCA_MODELS.why: Links to COPD self-management, mood follow-up and reversibility

SCA_MODELS.text: Just so we’re clear: until the form is done, if you’re unwell with your chest, you get help exactly as before — 999 if you’re very breathless or have chest pain. Can you tell me the plan back, in your own words?
SCA_MODELS.why: Clarifies the interim position and checks understanding

SCA_MODELS.text: Face to face this week, Michael with me if he’ll come. The form covers the restart only — everything else carries on. Copy where it can be seen, flagged to the ambulance people. I can change my mind any time.
Exactly right. Reception will ring you today with a double appointment. Is there anything else you wanted to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Books follow-up and shares the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you, doctor. I’ve been carrying that for a year.

SCA_STEM.name: Stanley Kerr
pmh: Severe COPD — FEV1 28% predicted, home nebulisers, two admissions last winter
meds: Inhaled and nebulised COPD treatment (see repeat list)
SCA_STEM.recent: Widowed, lives independently. Son Michael (52) visits on Sundays. No ReSPECT or DNACPR record on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone appointment booked by the patient: “wants to discuss resuscitation paperwork — asked to speak to the doctor.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Mental Capacity Act 2005 · GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010) · BMA, Resuscitation Council UK and RCN Decisions relating to CPR (2016) · NICE NG115 (COPD) · NICE NG222 (depression)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A patient with capacity who does not want CPR is entitled to refuse it, and his family cannot overturn that. Confirm capacity, screen mood, correct the belief that DNACPR stops other treatment, and turn a secret form into a shared conversation.

points.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: presume capacity; he must be able to understand, retain, use and weigh the information, and communicate a decision. This is usually demonstrable in the conversation itself — say so and record it.

Distinguish a values-based refusal from depression: ask about sleep, appetite, enjoyment, hopelessness and thoughts of ending life (NICE NG222). Future plans and intact pleasures point away from depression.

A DNACPR decision is about cardiopulmonary resuscitation only. Antibiotics, nebulisers, admission, non-invasive ventilation and all other treatment continue unless separately decided. ReSPECT records the wider picture in the patient’s own words.

A capacitous patient’s refusal of CPR must be respected; relatives are not decision-makers and cannot overturn it. Tracey (2014) requires patients to be involved in DNACPR decisions; Winspear (2015) requires consulting those close to a patient who lacks capacity. Sharing with family needs his consent.

The recorded decision guides clinicians. A legally binding refusal of life-sustaining treatment for a future loss of capacity is an advance decision (MCA 2005 ss24–26): written, signed, witnessed, and stating it applies even if life is at risk.
Survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is low in general and poorer with severe lung and heart disease; survivors may have lasting harm. Give this as information, not persuasion.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let him make the request in full; acknowledged its weight; set an agenda that included his son.
Independence, widowhood, pigeons and family, the relationship with Michael, two winter admissions.
“He’ll try”, “rehearsed in the mirror” and “a little less of me comes home”; asked what lay behind the timing.
Idea (form in a drawer; doctors stop trying); concern (Walter’s ICU death; Michael overturning it); expectation (a signed form, legal certainty, help telling Michael).
Face-to-face review this week; mood assessment; review of COPD and heart failure plans.
Values-based decision versus depression or coercion; understanding of scope.
Mood screen including hopelessness and thoughts of ending life; interim safety-net for chest deterioration.
Stated he has capacity and that the request is a considered, values-based decision.
ReSPECT completed face to face; visible copy; record and ambulance flag; correct law on family; confidentiality respected; three-way conversation offered.
COPD winter plan and rescue medicines, heart failure review, bereavement.
Appointment booked; reversible at any time; 999 for acute deterioration meanwhile; open door if low.

social.t: His brother’s ICU death drives the timing; his son’s fear shows as control. Name both, and offer support for the family conversation.
A widower living alone with pigeons and a granddaughter’s graduation ahead: the decision is about the manner of dying, not a wish to die.

legal.t: Capacity is presumed and decision-specific. A capacitous refusal of CPR must be respected; relatives cannot overturn it. An advance decision to refuse treatment (ss24–26) makes a future refusal of life-sustaining treatment legally binding if it meets the formal requirements.

Tracey v Cambridge University Hospitals (2014): patients must be involved in DNACPR decisions. Winspear v City Hospitals Sunderland (2015): those close to a patient who lacks capacity must be consulted.
GMC Confidentiality (2017): do not share with his son without his consent.

professional.h: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010)
professional.t: Discuss CPR sensitively, give honest information about likely outcomes, and record decisions so they can be found by others.
A decision is only useful if it can be found: copy in the house, flagged on the GP record, and shared with out-of-hours and ambulance services.

community.t: ReSPECT patient information (Resuscitation Council UK), Compassion in Dying for advance decisions, Asthma and Lung UK for COPD support, Cruse for bereavement.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of it as switching off one specific thing — the chest-pumping restart at the very end — while all the other switches stay on.”

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The form is the easy half of this station. It is failed on wrong law, missed mood screening, and a doctor who either argues with the decision or accepts it without finding Walter and the plan to keep it secret.

items.fail: Telling him his family must agree, or that a doctor decides for him.
items.why: A capacitous patient’s refusal of CPR stands; relatives are not decision-makers. Wrong law is a Tasks fail.
items.fix: “This is yours to decide. Michael cannot overturn it. Families are told with your permission.”

items.fail: Agreeing to the form without screening mood or confirming capacity.
items.why: A treatment refusal can be a sign of depression; examiners expect you to check and say so.
items.fix: Brief mood screen (sleep, enjoyment, hopelessness, thoughts of ending life) and state capacity aloud.

items.fail: Not correcting the belief that DNACPR stops all treatment.
items.why: It has delayed his request for a year and would affect his future choices.
items.fix: Explain CPR only; everything else continues. Offer ReSPECT for the wider picture.

items.why: Walter’s ICU death is the driver; missing it loses the emotional core.
items.fix: Ask about the timing and let him tell the story.

items.fail: Colluding with the drawer plan, or phoning Michael yourself.
items.why: One risks lasting harm to the family; the other breaches confidentiality.
items.fix: Test the plan with a question and offer a supported three-way conversation, with his consent.

items.fail: Completing everything by phone and ending with “I’ll send you the form.”
items.why: A decision the ambulance service cannot see does not protect him.
items.fix: Face-to-face appointment, visible copy, record and ambulance flags, and reversibility stated.
